sentences.text: Cladoselache possessed a streamlined body and deeply forked tail similar to modern mako and great white sharks, though it was not closely related to them. This agile marine predator grew to several meters in length, featuring a tapered, keeled tail that ended in a crescent-shaped caudal fin.

Evidence indicates the animal had at least five pairs of slender, well-separated branchial arches, resulting in five gill slits on each side. All fins except the tail had a wide base continuous with the torso and were supported by cartilaginous rods called radials.

Its slender, smooth-edged teeth were adapted for grasping prey rather than tearing or chewing. The creature had a weak jaw joint compared to modern sharks, which was compensated by very powerful jaw muscles.
Fossils of Cladoselache were discovered in the Cleveland Shale on the south shore of Lake Erie.
Remains of this species have also been found in both North America and Europe.

Stomach contents preserved in fossils indicate it was a predator that ate small ray-finned fishes, thylacocephalan arthropods, conodonts, and hagfish-like proto-vertebrates. The presence of fish remains found tail-first in these stomachs suggests it was a fast and agile hunter.
Its long, slender cylindrical body and tail shape suggest it was a fierce predator that swam quickly and with great agility.

Cladoselache is considered an early member of the Chondrichthyes, the group of cartilaginous fish, but it is not a member of the modern shark group (Selachii), which evolved later in the Jurassic Period. It is often described as a basal chondrichthyan rather than a true shark.

Recent studies suggest it is closely related to symmoriiforms based on distinctive traits of its chondrocranium, dorsal fin spines, and pectoral fin bases. It may belong to an early-diverging clade at the base of Chondrichthyes or Elasmobranchii alongside symmoriiforms.
Cladoselache lived during the Late Devonian period, specifically from 372.15 to 358.86 million years ago during the Famennian stage.

Early sources suggested Cladoselache might have had six or seven gill slits, but this has not been confirmed. There is a debate regarding whether Cladoselache was the earliest-diverging member of Chondrichthyes or an elasmobranch that originated after holocephalans. Some studies suggested it was a derived elasmobranch close to hybodonts and modern sharks, but this view was considered uncertain and unstable. An alternative hypothesis suggests Cladoselache lies on the holocephalan stem-group leading to modern chimaeras. It is debated whether Cladoselache and symmoriiforms are more closely related to chimaeras than to true sharks and rays.
